column1: # Corpus C — machine-generated code.
# Corpus B is idiomatic, reviewed, hand-written OSS. It systematically
# under-reports exactly the patterns the AI-quality rules exist for —
# `placeholder-implementation`, `todo-marker`, `test-without-assertion`,
# `swallowed-error` — because a maintained project does not leave `todo!()` in
# `main`. A rule audited only against B is audited against the population least
# likely to trip it.
# What is here is **codegen** output: SDKs and clients emitted by a generator.
# That is directly relevant to the path-exclusion question (issue #21) — it is
# the `frb_generated.rs` failure mode at scale — and it says close to nothing
# about LLM-authored *application* code, which is what issues #23 and #24 are
# actually about. A green result here must not be read as covering that.
# The LLM-authored half is deliberately empty rather than filled with plausible
# guesses. Adding to it means following the procedure in
# `docs/harden-corpus.md`: identify candidates by the artifacts agents leave
# (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .cursor/rules/, copilot-instructions.md), corroborate
# from commit trailers on at least 30% of the last 200 commits, filter to a
# permissive licence and a real project, hand-verify sampled files, and record
# the query and date here alongside the shas. Publishing the query is what makes
# the corpus auditable; publishing a list of repositories is not.
# Every row below is pinned to a commit (resolved 2026-08-31). A newly added row
# may carry a branch name for one commit: `harden.sh` records `pinned: false` for
# a non-sha ref and refuses to gate per-rule counts on that root, because a count
# measured against a moving branch is not reproducible and a gate built on one
# fires on somebody else's merge. Resolve with `git ls-remote <url> <branch>` and
# commit the sha before relying on its numbers.
# name
openapi-generator
google-cloud-python
aws-sdk-js-v3
# C2 — LLM-authored application code (added 2026-08-31)
# The rows above are *codegen*: a generator emitted them, and they say close to
# nothing about code an LLM wrote while a person watched. These ten are the
# other population, and they are the one issues #23 and #24 are actually about.
# The selection procedure, which matters more than the list — a list goes stale
# and a procedure can be re-run:
#   1. Identify by committed agent artifacts: CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md,
#      .cursor/rules/, .github/copilot-instructions.md, .aider.conf.yml.
#   2. Corroborate from history, which is harder to stage than a file:
#      `Co-Authored-By: Claude`, `Co-authored-by: Copilot`, `aider:` trailers
#      across recent commits. Recorded per repo below as a fraction, because a
#      squash-merging project hides trailers and a low fraction is evidence
#      about the merge strategy, not about the authorship.
#   3. Filter: permissive licence, substantial size in the target language,
#      real history, not a fork or a template.
#   4. Keep human-authored controls in the same set — `astro` and `vercel-ai`
#      here — or there is nothing to compare against.
# Trailer evidence at the pinned shas: spec-kit 42/50, crewai 25/50,
# openhands 19/50, aider 22/103, copilot-chat 8/50 plus committed Copilot
# instructions, vercel-ai 6/50, astro 6/50, stagehand 5/50, pydantic-ai 2/50,
# opencode 2/63. Seven of the ten commit a CLAUDE.md or an AGENTS.md.
# Our own agent-written repos are deliberately absent: they are corpus A, and
# using them here would be measuring the rules against the code they were
# written while looking at.
aider
spec-kit
crewai
openhands
copilot-chat
pydantic-ai
opencode
stagehand
vercel-ai
astro
